raw:
{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Autonomy" },
  "read": "Your kid is trying on who they are apart from you, and faith is one of the biggest identity markers a family carries. Announcing it at dinner is a statement, not just a preference — they want to be seen as someone whose inner life deserves to be taken seriously, not just corrected. The autonomy piece shows up in the bluntness of the announcement: they are staking a claim on their own story before you can manage it.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Lay down the rule — this family goes to church, end of discussion — which turns a faith question into a power struggle and almost guarantees they associate church with losing, not belonging." },
  "mentorMove": "Hold the expectation that faith and community matter in this family while treating their doubt as legitimate and worth a real conversation, so they feel respected rather than overruled.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "Our family takes faith seriously, and right now participation is part of what that looks like.",
    "This is a real conversation, not a veto — but you do not get to just opt out at dinner with no discussion."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Which service, which campus, which format, or whether they serve or just attend is all negotiable.",
    "A one-on-one conversation with a pastor, a different faith community, or a temporary arrangement while you talk it through can all be on the table."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 3, "label": "Collaboration" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I heard you tonight and I am not going to pretend I was not caught off guard. I am also not going to blow past what you said, because it matters that you said it out loud." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "I want to understand what is actually going on — not the headline, the real thing underneath it. Is it the belief part that feels shaky, or is it the sitting-in-a-pew-on-Sunday part, or something that happened there that bothered you? Because those are pretty different problems." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is where I land: I am not going to pretend you have no say in your own faith life, because that would be dishonest. But I am also not going to let a dinner announcement be the end of the conversation, because you are still part of this family and this is something our family does together. So let us figure out what a version of this looks like that we can both live with while you work through the bigger questions — because the questions are good ones and you deserve space to wrestle with them for real." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am holding you to staying in this conversation and staying connected to the community, because I have high standards for how we handle hard things and I know you are capable of doing it with honesty instead of just a walkout. That is what I am asking for — not blind agreement, just integrity in how we do this together." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Kids who feel steamrolled on identity questions often reject the thing entirely just to win back their selfhood. Kids who are taken seriously tend to come back to the values on their own terms. Stay curious over months, keep the door open on the hard questions, and resist the urge to treat every doubt as a crisis — the goal is that ten years from now they have a faith life they actually own, not one they escaped."
}
situation: My kid announced at dinner they are done with church and are not going anymore.
